hints: Every row must hold exactly one queen. So instead of choosing n squares out of n², what if you just choose a column for each row, one row at a time?
Backtracking row by row. Keep three boolean arrays: used columns, used r−c diagonals and used r+c anti-diagonals, so checking a square is O(1).

1. Start at row 0 with empty column/diagonal sets.
  2. For each column c in this row, skip it if c, r−c or r+c is already used.
  3. Otherwise place the queen, mark the three, and recurse to row r+1.
  4. When r == n, turn the chosen columns into strings and save the board.
  5. Unmark and try the next column.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every way to put n queens on n² squares (or every permutation of columns) and keep the valid boards.

approaches.name: Optimal: backtracking with O(1) checks
approaches.idea: Place one queen per row and prune immediately when a column or diagonal is taken, using three boolean arrays.
approaches.time: O(n!) roughly, plus O(n²) to build each board

explain: For n = 4, row 0 first tries column 0; every continuation hits a clash, so the search backs up. Row 0 = column 1 then forces row 1 = column 3, row 2 = column 0, row 3 = column 2, giving .Q.. / ...Q / Q... / ..Q.. The other board is its mirror, starting in column 2. Two squares share a diagonal exactly when r−c (or r+c) is equal, which is why those two numbers identify diagonals. Add n−1 to r−c so the array index is never negative.
recognize: 'Place items so that no two conflict' and 'return every arrangement' → constraint backtracking, one decision per row.
